main_damage_causes: Compression and removal of Lupin's moral self-reckoning (cowardice admission, 'I could have bitten any of you'), which strips his arc of its ethical spine and reduces his departure to external victimisation rather than principled accountability

The bridge-walk scene inverts and front-loads Lupin's emotional openness, collapsing his carefully guarded reserve into early sentimentality and replacing the incremental, earned intimacy of the office visits with a single expository monologue

The Shrieking Shack sequence diminishes Lupin's agency as moral brake and narrator of his own history, transferring his most important decisions and explanations to Harry and Sirius respectively, thereby weakening the audience's understanding of who Lupin truly is beneath the shabby robes

Systematic reduction of Lupin's voice and initiative in group scenes, particularly the Grimmauld Place dinner and political briefing, which transfers his intellectual and mediating function largely to Sirius
Loss of the escort and arrival sequence that re-establishes the Harry-Lupin mentoring relationship and shows Lupin as Harry's primary protector and guide in this film

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Bridge walk) – Lupin volunteers information about Lily unprompted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes no scene on a bridge where Lupin proactively opens up about Lily. Lupin's relationship with Harry develops gradually through office visits and Patronus lessons; he is warm but measured, and personal disclosures come cautiously (e.g., he admits knowing James only after Harry hears James's voice during the Patronus lesson, Scene 347-349).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin delivers an extended, emotionally effusive monologue about Lily – 'She was there for me at a time when no one else was... a singularly gifted witch... an uncommonly kind woman... she had a way of seeing the beauty in whoever she met' – unprompted, on their very first one-on-one conversation, before any trust has been established.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Book Lupin guards his past carefully; his emotional disclosures are earned and incremental, often reluctant (he deflects Harry's question about Sirius with 'You'd better be off', Scene 367). The film collapses his reserve into an open, almost sentimental confessor in their first private exchange, flattening a defining character trait – his careful, controlled self-presentation – and removing the earned quality of his later revelations about James and Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Bridge walk) – replaces the grindylow office visit and Snape's potion delivery
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 150-204 establish a rich private dynamic: Lupin invites Harry into his office to see the grindylow, makes tea, engages in cautious back-and-forth about the boggart decision, receives Snape's smoking potion (which seeds mystery about his condition), and deflects Harry's implicit suspicion of Snape with deliberate mildness. This sequence builds the mentor relationship through small, telling details.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The office visit with the grindylow, the tea, the Snape potion scene, and the nuanced dialogue about the boggart decision are entirely absent. Their first private conversation is the bridge walk, which substitutes a more overtly sentimental register.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The grindylow-office scene does significant character work: it shows Lupin's warmth expressed through domestic hospitality (tea, chocolate), his shrewdness in reading Harry, his careful loyalty to Snape despite provocation, and the mystery of the potion. Removing it strips texture from the mentor relationship and eliminates the audience's earliest signal of Lupin's secret condition through legitimate dramatic irony.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Boggart lesson) – Lupin steps in front of Harry with no prior private conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 138 establishes that after the class Harry is troubled and confused about why Lupin blocked him. The tension is resolved in the private office visit (Scenes 170-178) where Lupin explains he expected Voldemort and is impressed that Harry's deepest fear is fear itself – a psychologically resonant beat that also demonstrates Lupin's respect for Harry's inner life.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Boggart lesson plays out similarly but the resolution of why Lupin intervened is compressed into the bridge walk (Film Scene 7), where Lupin explains the Voldemort assumption and the 'what you fear most is fear' insight in a more casual register, folded into the larger Lily monologue rather than standing as its own earned discovery.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The separation between the classroom event and Lupin's explanation in the book gives both moments more weight. In the film the insight arrives in the same conversation as the Lily speech, diluting its impact. The damage is minor but real: it compresses a careful structural rhythm into a single expository walk.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Bridge walk lead-in) – Lupin approaches Harry unsolicited when Harry is left behind from Hogsmeade
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book it is Harry who seeks out Lupin (Scene 149-150); Lupin is in his office and Harry stumbles across him. The dynamic is Harry approaching the mentor, not the mentor seeking out the student.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin appears and calls to Harry from off-screen ('So. No Hogsmeade, eh?'), initiating the conversation and walking alongside Harry – a subtle but meaningful reversal of who pursues the relationship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but telling shift: book Lupin is warm but not pursuing; he responds to Harry rather than initiating. Making Lupin the pursuer here contributes to a slightly softer, more openly nurturing characterisation that the book deliberately avoids in favour of a more guarded mentor figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11-12 (Patronus lesson) – Harry's chosen memory is watching parents 'just talking'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 319-369 show Harry cycling through multiple memories (first broom ride, Gryffindor winning the Cup) before finally succeeding. The memory that works is never specified as a vision of his parents – the successful Patronus emerges from the third attempt with a happy memory Harry finds for himself. The emotional texture is Harry discovering what happiness means to him under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry tells Lupin his successful memory is an imagined scene of his parents talking to him – 'I was thinking of him. And Mum. Seeing their faces... I don't even know if it's real. But it's the best I have.' This is presented as the memory that produces the strong Patronus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Patronus lesson is partly about Harry's complicated grief: he must find joy powerful enough to overcome horror, and crucially he must not use the voices of his dying parents as his anchor (Scene 369). The film collapses this tension by making the successful memory literally about seeing his parents, which is thematically contradictory to the book's lesson and reduces the psychological complexity of what a Patronus requires. It also slightly sentimentalises Lupin's role as the teacher who facilitates this imagined reunion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13-14 (Marauder's Map corridor/office) – Lupin keeps the map and threatens Harry with it
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 433-440 show Lupin confiscating the map and refusing to return it, but the scene ends with Lupin walking away leaving Harry feeling 'worse by far than he had at any point in Snape's office' – a moment of genuine moral authority that slightly damages Harry's trust in him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reproduces the confiscation and the reprimand but adds a new beat: Lupin taps the map and warns Harry 'If you do [take detours]. I'll know.' The scene also has Lupin reacting to Harry mentioning Pettigrew on the Map with a barely perceptible hesitation before dismissing it – a film invention.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'I'll know' line gives Lupin a slightly surveillance-inflected edge inconsistent with his book characterisation. More importantly, the film's Lupin clearly registers 'Pettigrew' with visible alarm and then chooses to suppress it, which is a reasonable dramatic choice but makes him more calculatedly deceptive than the book, where his failure to act is framed as cowardice rather than active concealment in that moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Shrieking Shack) – Lupin immediately agrees to let Pettigrew die ('All right then. As you wish')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 518-523 shows Lupin physically restraining Black from killing Pettigrew and arguing strenuously that 'they've got a right to know everything' and 'you owe Harry the truth.' Only after a full explanation does Lupin stand shoulder to shoulder with Black to carry out the execution. His moral position is first to insist on truth and process, not summary killing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After Black says 'He dies. Now,' Lupin says 'Wait, Sirius –' but when Black delivers his 'I did my waiting!' speech, Lupin simply nods and says 'All right then. As you wish...' before Harry intervenes. The lengthy insistence on explanation, truth, and Harry's right to know is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the book's single clearest demonstration of Lupin's moral character under pressure: he controls his own desire for revenge and insists on justice over execution. Book Lupin's 'They've got a right to know everything – Ron's kept him as a pet – you owe Harry the truth' is not a delaying tactic but a genuine ethical position. The film's Lupin capitulates almost immediately, transferring the moral brake entirely to Harry. This materially damages Lupin's characterisation as a man whose defining quality is doing the right thing even when it's costly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Shrieking Shack) – Lupin's self-reproach about cowardice regarding Sirius's Animagus status is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 564-566 contain Lupin's extended self-indictment: 'All this year, I have been battling with myself... I didn't do it. Why? Because I was too cowardly... and so I convinced myself that Sirius was getting into the school using dark arts... so, in a way, Snape's been right about me all along.' This is a crucial moment of moral self-awareness and links directly to the book's themes about the costs of self-deception.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent speech appears in the film corpus. Lupin's explanation in the Shrieking Shack is compressed; the admission of cowardice and the acknowledgment that Snape had a point about his untrustworthiness are not present.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This self-reproach is arguably the most important piece of Lupin's internal arc in the entire book: it connects his personal flaw (prioritising self-preservation over responsibility) to the near-tragedy that almost occurred, and it gives his departure at the end genuine moral weight. Without it, Lupin resigns for external reasons (the werewolf reveal) rather than also having been confronted with his own failure of nerve. The film loses a complete arc beat that contextualises everything Lupin does and fails to do throughout the year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Shrieking Shack) – the backstory of the Marauders is told almost entirely by Sirius, not Lupin
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 539-573 have Lupin lead the explanation of the Marauders' history – how his transformations worked, how his friends became Animagi, the story of Snape's near-death. It is explicitly Lupin's story to tell: 'All right... but you'll need to help me, Sirius. I only know how it began.' Lupin is the narrator of his own past.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this backstory significantly. Key elements – the years it took to become Animagi, Peter's role, the near misses with the werewolf, Lupin's guilt about Dumbledore's trust – are either cut or delivered as brief exchanges mostly driven by Black. The Snape prank backstory is also cut.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Marauders' backstory is where the audience understands who Lupin was before he became the shabby, careful teacher – a boy who inspired fierce loyalty, who was gifted with friends who transformed themselves for him, and who carries deep guilt about the consequences. Compressing this and redistributing narrative agency to Black diminishes Lupin's ownership of his own history and weakens the emotional logic of his partnership with Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Lupin's office, departure) – the Marauder's Map return and Invisibility Cloak return are collapsed/altered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 759-761 show Lupin returning both the Invisibility Cloak and the Marauder's Map, explicitly saying 'I am no longer your teacher, so I don't feel guilty about giving you back this as well.' He also makes a wry joke about James wanting Harry to know the secret passages. This scene is a graceful, bittersweet coda that crystallises Lupin's relationship with Harry and his connection to James.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Lupin returns only the Map, saying 'Mischief managed' and clearing it with his wand before departing. The Cloak is not mentioned. The joke about James wanting Harry to find the secret passages is absent. The farewell is shorter and less resonant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The double return of Cloak and Map in the book is symbolically loaded: Lupin is passing on James's legacy to Harry in two forms, with a final wink that connects his old mischief-making self to the present. The film's version is more functional and melancholy but loses the warmth and the explicit articulation of what Lupin is passing on – both materially and in spirit. This slightly diminishes the farewell's emotional payoff.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Lupin's office, departure) – Lupin's resignation framing omits self-blame
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 751: Lupin says 'I could have bitten any of you.... That must never happen again.' He takes personal moral responsibility for the danger he posed, not just citing external pressure from parents.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Lupin says 'people like me, well... let's just say I'm used to this by now' – framing his departure as social persecution he has resigned himself to, not as an ethical response to his own failure the previous night.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The shift from 'I could have bitten any of you' to 'I'm used to this' transforms Lupin's departure from an act of moral accountability into victimhood. Both are true in the books, but the film emphasises only the latter. This softens a key character note: book Lupin holds himself to a higher standard than society holds him, which is part of what makes him admirable despite his failures.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Headquarters briefing: Lupin delivers single expository line about Fudge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Lupin as an active, multi-voiced participant in the Grimmauld Place political discussion: he offers nuanced analysis of goblin loyalties (Scenes 70-71), explains Ministry dynamics at length (Scenes 97, 99, 103), mediates the Molly/Sirius argument with authority and sharp intelligence (Scenes 78, 81, 83), and demonstrates sophisticated political thinking throughout the dinner scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin delivers a single two-sentence explanation ('The Minister thinks Dumbledore's after his job... Fudge isn't in his right mind. Fear makes people do terrible things') and then disappears from the conversation. All substantive analysis is handed to Sirius.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Lupin is the room's quiet intellectual anchor — measured, analytically precise, and politically astute. The film reduces him to a single functional line before ceding the floor entirely, stripping his voice and undermining the impression that he is a thinker of equal or greater depth than Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Headquarters briefing: Lupin absent from Molly/Sirius argument over informing Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 78-84 are a defining Lupin moment: he intervenes in the Molly/Sirius standoff with quiet authority, tells Sirius to sit down, argues that Harry deserves the facts and is old enough to decide for himself, and then personally manages the fallout (silencing Mrs. Black's portrait). He acts as the room's adult moderator, respected by all parties.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Molly/Sirius argument occurs in the film but Lupin plays no mediating role. He is present but silent; the argument resolves without his intervention.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Lupin's clearest demonstrations of social authority and emotional intelligence in the books. His absence from the mediation role not only removes his agency but also damages the audience's understanding of why the Order respects him and why Harry trusts him. The relationship dynamic between Lupin, Sirius, and Molly is flattened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Arrival at Grimmauld Place: Lupin absent from escort and orientation of Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 10-57 show Lupin as Harry's primary point of contact throughout the entire rescue and escort sequence: he verifies Harry's identity, leads him through the house, explains travel logistics, writes the letter to the Dursleys, gives commands at key moments ('Mount your brooms,' 'Second signal, let's go'), covers Harry from below during flight, and personally guides him into Grimmauld Place with whispered instructions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire escort sequence. Moody dominates what little is shown; Lupin has no identifiable leadership role in the arrival. The careful, attentive shepherding of Harry by Lupin is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The escort sequence is the primary vehicle for re-establishing Harry and Lupin's relationship after a year apart and showing Lupin's protective, mentoring function. Losing it means the audience has no foundation for Harry's trust in Lupin and no sense of their bond being renewed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Department of Mysteries: Lupin grabs Harry after Sirius falls through the veil
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 263-282 are an extended, emotionally intricate sequence: Lupin physically restrains Harry, speaks to him repeatedly with a voice 'breaking,' acknowledges his own grief while prioritizing Harry's safety, drags Harry away from the dais, and then immediately pivots to practical care (healing Neville, organizing the group). His restraint of Harry is an act of agonized love, not just physical force.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2 shows Lupin grabbing Harry as Harry tries to follow Sirius, and Harry struggling free to chase Bellatrix. The physical action is present but the emotional texture — Lupin's breaking voice, his repeated attempts to reach Harry verbally, his own visible grief — is absent. The scene is rapid and action-focused.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this moment to do double work: it shows Lupin's grief over losing his last Marauder friend while simultaneously establishing his selfless focus on Harry. The film retains the physical beat but loses the emotional register that makes it meaningful, reducing a complex grief-and-duty scene to a blocking action.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Headquarters: Lupin's werewolf marginalization and social cost entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 102 has Lupin note with dry self-awareness that he is 'not a very popular dinner guest with most of the community' due to being a werewolf, and Scene 169 (via Sirius) explains that Umbridge's legislation makes it nearly impossible for him to find work. His shabbiness is explicitly linked to economic exclusion. This is foundational to understanding his character's vulnerability and the wizarding world's prejudice.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No reference is made to Lupin's werewolf status in the film's Order scenes. His shabby appearance (referenced in film dialogue implicitly through costume) carries no explained social context. The prejudice theme and its personal cost to Lupin are never surfaced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's werewolf condition is not incidental flavor — it is his defining structural vulnerability and explains his poverty, his outsider status, and ultimately his arc in later books. Omitting any acknowledgment of it in the Order context means the audience cannot appreciate the personal stakes of his service or the institutional cruelty he navigates.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — No equivalent to Lupin's Occlumency intervention or mentoring of Harry outside formal settings
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 194 shows Lupin taking Harry aside at King's Cross to stress the critical importance of Occlumency lessons, lowering his voice and speaking with genuine urgency: 'Harry, there is nothing so important as you learning Occlumency. Do you understand me? Nothing.' Book Scenes 246-251 show him forcefully insisting Snape must resume lessons when Harry reports they have ended. These scenes establish Lupin as an active advocate for Harry's safety even when not physically present.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene exists in the film corpus. Lupin gives no private counsel to Harry about Occlumency or any other urgent matter.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These moments establish that Lupin's mentorship of Harry is proactive and persistent, not just reactive. His absence from this function in the film means the audience sees him only as a background Order member rather than as someone who actively works to protect Harry's future.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Prefect/Marauder reminiscence scene absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 128-130 contain Lupin's self-deprecating disclosure that he was made prefect to control James and Sirius and 'failed dismally' — a moment of warmth, humility, and humor that simultaneously illuminates his school-era character, his friendship with James, and his relationship with Sirius. It directly benefits Harry by reframing his father.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene in the film corpus. Lupin's humor, self-deprecation, and Marauder-era warmth are not given any comparable outlet.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is a small but telling window into the Lupin the books insist upon: witty, honest about his own failures, and capable of warmth. Its absence contributes to the cumulative flattening of his personality in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Lupin's post-veil grief and leadership of injured friends absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 279-282 show Lupin, despite his own grief, immediately assuming a leadership and healing role: he casts 'Finite' to end the spell on Neville's legs, organizes the group to find the others, speaks in a measured way while visibly in pain ('It sounded as though every word was causing him pain'). This balance of personal anguish and duty is defining.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After Harry breaks free to chase Bellatrix, Lupin has no further visible role in the Department of Mysteries sequence. The post-veil regrouping and his composed-amid-grief leadership are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the post-veil minutes to show Lupin at his most admirable: personally devastated but functionally present for others. Losing this beat means the audience never sees the full cost of Sirius's death on Lupin, nor his extraordinary discipline in the face of it.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Christmas party conversation about Snape/Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin engages in a nuanced, multi-beat exchange with Harry about Snape. He acknowledges the complexity of his own feelings ('I neither like nor dislike Severus'), explains why he trusts Snape despite personal history (the Wolfsbane Potion), credits Snape for keeping him healthy, and gently chides Harry for inherited prejudice while remaining warm and empathetic. He reasons from evidence and personal experience, not blind institutional loyalty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses Lupin's nuanced reasoning into a blunt authority-deferral ('It comes down to whether or not you trust Dumbledore's judgement. He trusts Snape. Therefore, I do.') and then turns sharply dismissive ('You're blinded by hatred... You are!'). The personal history with Snape, the Wolfsbane explanation, the acknowledgment of his own complicated feelings, and the warm paternal tone are all absent. Lupin sounds like a functionary enforcing a party line rather than a man reasoning from lived experience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's defining intellectual and emotional texture — the ability to hold contradictions, to reason honestly, to be self-aware about his own bias — is replaced with sharp institutional deflection. This makes him seem dogmatic rather than wise, and removes the most characterful material in the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Lupin's line 'You're blinded by hatred' / sharp rebuke of Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin says 'You are determined to hate him, Harry' with 'a faint smile' — a gentle, understanding observation that acknowledges Harry's inherited prejudice without hostility. The tone is paternal and empathetic, not confrontational.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Lupin snap 'You're blinded by hatred' and then follow it with a sharp, almost scolding speech ('You are! People are disappearing, Harry. Daily.'). The parenthetical stage direction even marks it '(sharply)'. This transforms a moment of gentle wisdom into a reprimand.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The shift from 'faint smile' and empathy to a sharp rebuke meaningfully alters Lupin's relational register with Harry. Book Lupin corrects with warmth; film Lupin scolds. This undermines the mentor-figure dynamic and makes him feel adversarial toward Harry rather than allied.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Absence of Lupin's werewolf mission/Greyback revelation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book Christmas scene contains the pivotal revelation that Lupin has been living undercover among werewolves on Dumbledore's orders, describes the personal cost ('I bear the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards'), introduces Fenrir Greyback and his ideology in detail, and culminates in Lupin revealing that Greyback was the werewolf who bit him as a child. This is the central scene establishing Lupin's arc, his self-sacrifice, and the personal stakes of his condition.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Christmas party scene contains none of this material. The entire werewolf-mission subplot, Greyback's introduction through Lupin's personal testimony, and the revelation about Lupin's own childhood attack are absent from the film corpus. Lupin appears only as a sounding board for the Snape/Malfoy debate.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most substantial loss in the corpus. The werewolf mission is Lupin's primary narrative function in HBP — it explains his haggard appearance, establishes his personal sacrifice for the Order, contextualizes his self-deprecation about being 'too dangerous,' and gives the Tonks relationship its full emotional weight. Without it, Lupin's characterization in the film is hollowed of its entire internal arc. Greyback also loses his most important contextual framing — the personal connection to Lupin that makes the Bill attack later resonate differently.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Absence of Half-Blood Prince conversation (Lupin's Hogwarts reminiscence)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has a warm, extended exchange in which Harry asks Lupin about the Half-Blood Prince, Lupin reminisces about Levicorpus being a craze in his fifth year, gently deflects Harry's hope that the Prince is James, confirms it wasn't Sirius or himself, and shares a fond memory ('Sometimes you remind me a lot of James. He called it my furry little problem in company'). This scene is rich with characterization: Lupin's wit, his warmth toward Harry, his connection to James's memory, and his self-deprecating humor about being a werewolf.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene exists in the film corpus. The entire Half-Blood Prince conversation with Lupin is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'furry little problem' exchange is one of the most characterful Lupin moments in HBP — it shows his wit, his ease with his condition, his bond with Harry through James's memory, and his subtle emotional intelligence. Its absence removes a key beat of the Harry-Lupin relationship and flattens Lupin's personality considerably.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Mr. Weasley's 'You'll have to forgive Remus. It takes its toll — his condition'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Lupin's haggard appearance and difficult circumstances through Lupin's own words and actions — his undercover mission, his self-aware commentary on bearing 'the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards,' and his quiet dignity in describing hardship. His condition is something he narrates and owns.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Mr. Weasley explains Lupin's behavior to Harry as though Lupin is a problem to be managed or excused ('You'll have to forgive Remus'). Lupin himself says nothing and is not present in the scene. His inner life is rendered as an external condition observed and interpreted by others.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Having Arthur apologize for Lupin's behavior rather than letting Lupin speak for himself reduces him to a passive figure whose condition is something others react to. This passivization is the opposite of the book's portrayal, where Lupin actively articulates his own situation with intelligence and self-awareness.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 3-7 - Burrow attack sequence; Lupin present but functionally passive
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Burrow attack does not occur in the book in this form; however, the corpus establishes Lupin as an active fighter — at Hogwarts he battles Death Eaters, pursues Snape, gives detailed tactical accounts of the fighting, and is specifically noted as combating a separate Death Eater. His physical courage and role as a capable Order fighter is consistently established.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the attack sequence, Lupin draws his wand and races after Harry (Film Scene 6), and appears in the clearing at the end (Film Scene 7), but has no spoken lines, takes no decisive action, and is simply one figure among the Weasley crowd who arrives after Harry and Ginny have already subdued Greyback. He is present but functionally invisible.
damaging_scenes.explanation: An invented film action scene that includes Lupin but gives him no agency or dialogue further cements a pattern of Lupin as passive background presence. Given that the book establishes him as a capable, active fighter and tactician, this is a missed opportunity that compounds the overall passivization of the character.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Sitting room/kitchen after Seven Potters (Film Scene 2): Lupin jokes about Bill's werewolf diet
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Lupin at this gathering as 'grayer, more lined' — present but subdued. The wedding announcement from Tonks is interrupted by Moody. Lupin does not make jokes at the expense of Bill's werewolf condition. Book Lupin is acutely sensitive about werewolf affliction; he later agonizes that his condition has ruined Tonks's life and risks their child.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Lupin quips to Fleur: 'Just remember, Fleur, once you're married: Bill takes his steaks on the raw side now.' This is a breezy, self-confident joke about werewolf nature made in company.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Book Lupin is defined by deep shame and anguish about his condition — it is what drove him to believe he should never have married Tonks and should not have fathered a child. A casual public joke about werewolf appetites is fundamentally inconsistent with that characterization and softens the psychological weight of his condition before the Grimmauld Place confrontation.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Sitting room/kitchen after Seven Potters (Film Scene 2): Tonks announces the pregnancy, Lupin's reaction absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not show the pregnancy announced at the Seven Potters gathering. The pregnancy is revealed much later, at Grimmauld Place, where Lupin delivers the news with 'an air of forcing himself to admit something unpleasant' and gives 'an artificial smile that was more like a grimace.' His torment about the pregnancy is the emotional core of the Grimmauld Place scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Tonks begins to announce 'Remus and I are --' at the pre-flight gathering, cut off by Moody. Lupin stands by with apparent affection ('staring at Tonks with affection'). The film later places the godfather offer at the wedding scene (Film Scene 7) where Lupin 'grins' and 'claps Harry on the shoulder,' presenting the pregnancy and godfather offer as warm, untroubled news.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's entire Grimmauld Place crisis — Lupin's self-loathing about the pregnancy, his attempt to abandon Tonks and the unborn child, Harry's furious confrontation — depends on the audience understanding that Lupin experienced the pregnancy as a catastrophe rather than a joy. By presenting him as warmly affectionate and having the godfather offer delivered with a grin, the film strips away the psychological groundwork for the book's most important Lupin scene. The emotional arc from shame to reconciliation is destroyed before it can begin.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Sitting room after Seven Potters: Lupin's interrogation of Harry (Film Scene 4)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Lupin 'grabbed Harry by the upper arm and dragged him, none too gently, back into the kitchen' — a controlled but forceful action. He then administers the verification question with a 'small shake,' releases Harry, and 'fell back against a kitchen cupboard.' The physicality is present but restrained; Lupin is terse and urgent but not theatrical.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Lupin 'grabs a fistful of his shirt and hurls him against the wall' — a considerably more violent gesture. Ginny shouts 'Remus! What're you doing!' as if witnessing something alarming rather than a security measure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor amplification of physical violence that slightly distorts Lupin's characteristic controlled intensity, but the scene retains its essential function and explanation. Damage is limited.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Kitchen at Burrow: entire Expelliarmus confrontation absent from film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains a substantial scene (Book Scenes 39–47) in which Lupin confronts Harry about using Expelliarmus against Death Eaters, arguing with 'painful restraint' that it was 'close to suicidal.' Harry pushes back, invoking his moral code ('I won't blast people out of my way just because they're there — that's Voldemort's job'). Lupin is making Harry 'feel idiotic' yet Harry holds his defiant grain. This exchange defines both characters: Lupin as a tactically-minded adult who can be wrong about Harry's instincts, Harry as someone whose moral identity resists pressure even from mentors.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange does not appear in the film corpus. After the security verification the scene moves directly to Kingsley's arrival in the yard.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most character-rich Lupin scenes in the book. It shows Lupin in productive conflict with Harry — wrong in a way that illuminates his pragmatism versus Harry's principled core — and it establishes Expelliarmus as Harry's deliberate moral signature, which pays off at the final duel. Losing it removes a significant dimension of the mentor–student relationship and flattens Lupin to a pure ally rather than a figure capable of instructive friction with Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Burrow yard vigil: Lupin's emotional reaction to Tonks's return (Film Scene 5)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 76: 'Tonks cried as she staggered off the broom into Lupin's arms. His face was set and white: He seemed unable to speak.' Book Scene 82: 'Lupin sounded almost angry at Tonks' when asking what kept her. Book Scene 84: 'A muscle was jumping in Lupin's jaw. He nodded, but seemed unable to say anything else.' This is a brief but potent portrait of a man whose terror and love are expressed as barely-suppressed fury — consistent with the book's Lupin who conceals overwhelming emotion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ron and Tonks returning (Film Scene 5), but Lupin's specific emotional response — the white face, the near-anger, the jaw muscle — is not rendered. The scene focuses on Ron and Hermione's reunion.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's micro-portrait of Lupin's reaction to Tonks's return is one of the few moments that shows his emotional depth toward her without dialogue. Its absence contributes to the film's overall thinning of the Lupin–Tonks relationship as an emotionally complex bond.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Burrow sitting room: Lupin's 'You think like James' exchange and Mad-Eye toast (Film Scene 6)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 100–113: Lupin raises the question of Mundungus's possible betrayal; Harry defends his trust in the Order. Lupin gives Harry a pitying look and says 'I think you're like James — who would have regarded it as the height of dishonor to mistrust his friends,' explicitly evoking Pettigrew's betrayal of James. Harry feels 'irrationally angry.' Lupin then immediately pivots to action: 'There's work to do' and volunteers to retrieve Mad-Eye's body with Bill.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 6, after Bill announces Mad-Eye's death and Mundungus's flight, Harry makes the trust speech ('I trust everyone in this room') and Lupin simply says 'Understood.' The James comparison, the pitying look, the implied Pettigrew reference, and the body-retrieval mission are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The James comparison is one of the few places where Lupin's unique position as both James's friend and Harry's mentor is made explicit and emotionally operative. Replacing his complex, slightly patronizing observation with a single word of deference ('Understood') flattens his characterization and removes the intergenerational emotional texture the books sustain.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Grimmauld Place: entire Lupin confrontation scene absent from film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 126–253: Lupin visits Grimmauld Place, reveals the pregnancy with grimacing discomfort, offers to abandon Tonks and join Harry's mission, and is confronted by Harry in a prolonged and explosive scene. Harry calls him a coward, accuses him of wanting to step into Sirius's shoes, and says he'd be ashamed of him. Lupin draws his wand and blasts Harry against the wall before storming out. Harry reflects on whether it was worth it and hopes Lupin will go back to Tonks. This is Lupin's central arc scene — his lowest moral moment and the crucible through which he becomes the redeemed father who dies at the Battle of Hogwarts.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Grimmauld Place scene does not appear in the film corpus at all. Lupin is seen in the wedding scene (Film Scene 7) offering the godfather role warmly, and next appears at Hogwarts during the battle (Film Scenes 9–13). The entire crisis of abandonment, shame, and Harry's intervention is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the film's treatment of Lupin. The Grimmauld Place confrontation is his entire character arc in Deathly Hallows: it establishes his self-destructive shame about his werewolf nature, his temptation to flee responsibility, Harry's moral courage in refusing to collude, and the stakes of his eventual reconciliation with Tonks and joy at Teddy's birth. Without it, Lupin's death at the Battle of Hogwarts carries no arc weight — he is simply a peripheral ally who dies, rather than a man who chose to stay and fight for the family he almost abandoned. The Shell Cottage scene (birth of Teddy, godfather offer) also loses most of its emotional resonance because the preceding crisis is unknown to the film audience.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Potterwatch broadcast: Lupin's radio appearance reduced/absent as narrative beat
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 266–278: Ron reveals that Lupin is the voice 'Romulus' on Potterwatch. Lupin states his firm belief that Harry is alive, delivers the line 'I'd tell him to follow his instincts, which are good and nearly always right' — a direct reversal of his earlier Expelliarmus criticism — and Harry feels 'a mixture of gratitude and shame,' wondering if Lupin has forgiven him. This is the resolution beat of the Grimmauld Place arc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Potterwatch sequence does not appear in the film corpus provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Even if the Grimmauld Place scene were present, Potterwatch provides the emotional resolution: Lupin's public endorsement of Harry's instincts implicitly walks back his criticism and signals reconciliation. Its absence means there is no closure to an arc that the film has already eliminated — compounding the damage by removing both the conflict and its resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Shell Cottage: Teddy's birth and godfather offer (Film Scene 7, placed at wedding instead)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 281–305: Lupin arrives at Shell Cottage in a state of transported joy, 'dazed by his own happiness,' looking 'years younger than Harry had ever seen him,' hugs Harry spontaneously, and asks him to be godfather. He stays for wine and describes the baby's changing hair color with delight before reluctantly departing. The scene's emotional power comes entirely from the contrast with his earlier despair in Grimmauld Place.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film relocates the godfather offer to the wedding scene in DH Part 1 (Film Scene 7), where Lupin says 'We want you to be the godfather,' 'grins, claps Harry on the shoulder and hikes off into the darkness.' The Shell Cottage birth scene is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moving the godfather offer from its book position (after reconciliation, after Teddy's actual birth) to before the Grimmauld Place crisis inverts the narrative logic entirely. In the book the offer is the culmination of Lupin's redemption — having chosen to stay with Tonks and face fatherhood, he is exuberant and renewed. In the film it is made as a warm social gesture at a wedding, with no weight of earned growth behind it. The arc from shame to joy is collapsed into a single cheerful transaction.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Battle of Hogwarts battlements: Lupin's invented aphorism (Film Scene 11)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not give Lupin a philosophical speech at the battle. His role is functional: he is assigned to lead fighters into the grounds (Book Scene 324). His characterization in the battle is defined by action and by others' anxiety about his whereabouts, not by maxims.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Lupin delivers an invented line: 'It's the quality of one's conviction that determines success, not the number of one's followers.' When Kingsley asks who said that, Lupin replies 'Me,' and they share a 'fatalistic smile.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line is not damaging in isolation but it is symptomatic of the film's substitution of aphoristic gravitas for the book's more interior and conflicted Lupin. It is a minor voice inconsistency.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Battle of Hogwarts: Tonks's arrival at the battle (cut scene — treated as absent per instructions)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 326: Tonks appears at Hogwarts having left Teddy with Andromeda, searching desperately for Lupin. Book Scene 329: She is told Lupin was dueling Dolohov. Their deaths are discovered together (Book Scene 330), fingers intertwined. The arc of two people who chose each other and their cause over safety — after nearly being separated by Lupin's self-loathing — is completed.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction, the Tonks-arrives-at-battle scene is cut from the theatrical release. In the theatrical film, Tonks appears in the battlements scenes (Film Scenes 11–13) but her desperate search for Lupin and the emotional stakes of their joint presence at the battle are not established for the audience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The theatrical cut removes the final active expression of the Lupin–Tonks relationship as a mutual choice. Their intertwined bodies in the Great Hall (Film Scene 14) carry emotional weight in the film, but without the Grimmauld Place arc and without Tonks's desperate search for him, the image is poignant rather than structurally meaningful. The relationship arc — from Lupin's attempted abandonment to their dying together — is incomplete.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Resurrection Stone scene in the Forest: Lupin's reduced dialogue (Film Scene 15)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 352–356: Lupin has substantive lines. He says 'And he will want it to be quick.' Harry addresses Lupin 'more than any of them, beseeching him,' apologizing specifically for Lupin dying 'right after you'd had your son.' Lupin responds: 'I am sorry too. Sorry I will never know him... but he will know why I died and I hope he will understand. I was trying to make a world in which he could live a happier life.' This is the thematic resolution of Lupin's entire arc — he has died not in flight but in the act of providing for his son.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Lupin says 'And he will want it to be quick' and later 'Others will tell him what his mother and father died for. Someday he'll understand...' Harry's specific, beseeching apology to Lupin about dying right after Teddy's birth is present ('And Remus, your son...') but Lupin's response is compressed and slightly generalized, losing the specific first-person sorrow ('Sorry I will never know him') that makes it personal rather than noble.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film retains the structural beat but softens the personal anguish. Book Lupin says 'Sorry I will never know him' — a father's grief. Film Lupin says 'Others will tell him' — a soldier's consolation. The shift from personal loss to philosophical acceptance is a characterization loss, though modest given the scene is otherwise present.
